result.markdown: --- title: ' **Week 1**: Getting started' subtitle: Biology Experimental Design and Analysis (BEDA) body-classes: manual-page toc: true toc-location: left toc-depth: 3 number-sections: false # number-depth: 2 --- ## Introduction Welcome to your first BEDA practical. As this is the first week of the semester we will simply take a moment to get you familiar with the unit of study and the practicals. ### Learning outcomes By the end of this practical, you should be able to: | Learning outcome | How you will practise it | |---|---| | Formulate a measurable biological question. | Use variables from the penguin or possum dataset to develop a question that can be investigated with data. See [Activity 2: Refine or formulate a biological question](#activity-2). | | Identify response and predictor variables in a research question. | Decide what you want to explain or compare, then identify the variable that may explain it. See [Activity 2](#activity-2). | | Classify the variables and express their relationship as `y ~ x`. | Examine the available variables, classify their types and write the proposed relationship as a simple model. See [Activity 1](#activity-1) and [Activity 2](#activity-2). | | Sketch a graphical model suited to the variables. | Choose a plot that matches the variable types, label its axes and sketch the expected pattern or comparison. See [Activity 3: Sketch the graphical model](#activity-3). | | Explain one limitation of the proposed model or dataset. | Review your proposed model and identify something the data or model may not adequately address. See [Activity 4: Check the model and discuss it](#activity-4). | ## [Workshop]{.manual-activity-label} Getting started (30 min) {.manual-activity #workshop-30-min} Workshop 1 is a guided activity that helps you get started with the software needed to analyse data in BEDA. It also introduces the empirical modelling approach which you can use to formulate a biological question, identify variables and sketch a graphical model. You will use the `penguin` and `possum` datasets to practise these skills. ## Quick recap: questions, variables and plots In the model notation `y ~ x`, `y` is the response and `x` is the predictor. In words, we are proposing that the response is related to, or explained by, the predictor. - Use a **scatterplot** when the response and predictor are both continuous. - Use a **boxplot** when the response is continuous and the predictor defines categories or groups. The [Week 1 lectures](../lectures/L01/index.qmd) explain the empirical modelling approach. [Workshop 1](w01-intro.qmd) provides the guided penguin example and the variable-pair checklist. Return to those pages if you need the full explanation rather than trying to reconstruct it here. ## Get ready - Your lab notebook, or an accessible digital document, for the Model Card and plot sketch - [penguins.csv](assets/penguins.csv) - [possums.xlsx](assets/possums.xlsx) - Jamovi, experienced R, or SPSS if your software is ready; software is optional for today's sketching task ## [Activity]{.manual-activity-label} Your task {.manual-activity #your-task} Your goal is to think like a research biologist: use the available variables to formulate a question, represent it as a simple model, and decide what a suitable plot would show. You do not need to fit or test a statistical model today. ### 1. Explore one dataset {#activity-1} Open `penguins.csv` or `possums.xlsx` and read the variable names. Identify at least one continuous variable and one possible predictor. **What to produce:** A short list of two or three variables you might use, with their variable types. **If you are stuck:** Start with `body_mass_g` and `species` in the penguin data, or `BW` and `Age` in the possum data. ### 2. Refine or formulate a biological question {#activity-2} Use your Workshop Model Card or begin a new one. State a measurable relationship or comparison and name the response and predictor. **What to produce:** A question plus the model written as `response ~ predictor` and explained in words. **If you are stuck:** Use the frame, “How does **response** differ with, or relate to, **predictor**?” ### 3. Sketch the graphical model {#activity-3} Choose a plot that matches the variable types, then sketch it in your notebook. Label both axes and show the pattern or group comparison you expect. **What to produce:** A labelled scatterplot or boxplot sketch. You may reproduce it in software, but the sketch is sufficient. **If you are stuck:** Recheck the two plot rules in the recap. A continuous response with a categorical predictor suggests a boxplot; two continuous variables suggest a scatterplot. ### 4. Check the model and discuss it {#activity-4} Explain why your plot suits the question and variable types. Then identify one limitation or unresolved question. Check your own Model Card or discuss it with a peer or demonstrator. **What to produce:** One reason for the plot choice and one careful limitation. **If you are stuck:** Begin with “This plot does not show…” or “I would need ___ before concluding…”. ::: {.callout-note} ## Example 1. Open the **possum data**. We will consider how possum **body weight** changes with **age**. 2. Body weight (`BW`) is continuous, while `Age` records age classes. A boxplot is therefore a reasonable starting point. 3. If exact age in years had been recorded as a continuous variable, a scatterplot could instead show how weight changes with age. 4. The model is `BW ~ Age`: body weight is related to, or explained by, age class. The code below produces the boxplot, but you are only required to sketch it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} library(readxl) possums <- read_excel("assets/possums.xlsx", sheet = 2) library(ggplot2) ggplot(possums, aes(x = Age, y = BW)) + geom_boxplot() + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](102-week01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-alt='Boxplot comparing possum body weight between juvenile and adult age classes.' width=672} ::: ::: The plot helps us plan an analysis, but it also exposes a problem: there is only one juvenile possum in the dataset. We could draw the comparison, but we could not analyse it reliably without more juvenile observations. **Food for thought:** Can age class still be useful in a model when one group contains only one animal? What additional data would you need? ::: ## That is a wrap! Keep your completed Model Card in your lab notebook. It records how you moved from a biological question to variables and a graphical model, and you will use the same reasoning throughout BEDA. If part of the task remains unclear, record the specific decision you were unsure about and ask a demonstrator or post on Ed. Next week we will build on this foundation when we examine study design and data structure. ## [Optional]{.manual-activity-label} Fancy a challenge? {.manual-activity .is-optional #fancy-a-challenge} This section is for students who finish early or want further practice. Use the penguin or possum data to draw plots and express models as `y ~ x`; you are not expected to fit the statistical models yet. 1. **Penguins dataset:** Explore the relationship among `bill_length_mm`, `bill_depth_mm`, and `flipper_length_mm`. Can one two-dimensional plot show all three clearly, or would you use more than one plot or another visual property? State the model or models in words. 2. **Possums dataset:** Explore the relationship between body weight (`BW`) and boldness (`BoldBLUP`). How might `Sex` and `Age` change that relationship? Sketch a way to show three variables together, then consider what would be lost or become difficult to read if you tried to show all four.
